entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen13960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13961" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> All the ways of a man <hi type="italic">are</hi> clean in his own eyes; but the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> weigheth the spirits. <div eID="gen13961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13962" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. We are all apt to be partial in judging of ourselves: <hi type="italic">All the ways of a man,</hi> all his designs, all his doings, <hi type="italic">are clean in his own eyes,</hi> and he sees nothing amiss in them, nothing for which to condemn himself, or which should make his projects prove otherwise than well; and therefore he is confident of success, and that the answer of the tongue shall be according to the expectations of the heart; but there is a great deal of pollution cleaving to our ways, which we are not aware of, or do not think so ill of as we ought. 2. The judgment of God concerning us, we are sure, is according to truth: He <hi type="italic">weighs the spirits</hi> in a just and unerring balance, knows what is in us, and passes a judgment upon us accordingly, writing <hi type="italic">Tekel</hi> upon that which passed our scale with approbation—<hi type="italic">weighed in the balance and found wanting;</hi> and by his judgment we must stand or fall. He not only sees men's ways but tries their spirits, and we are as our spirits are.

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen13962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13963" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> Commit thy works unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and thy thoughts shall be established. <div eID="gen13963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13964" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is a very desirable thing to have <hi type="italic">our thoughts established,</hi> and not tossed, and put into a hurry, by disquieting cares and fears,—to go on in an even steady course of honesty and piety, not disturbed, or put out of frame, by any event or change,—to be satisfied that all shall work for good and issue well at last, and therefore to be always easy and sedate. 2. The only way to have our <hi type="italic">thoughts established</hi> is to <hi type="italic">commit our works to the Lord.</hi> The great concerns of our souls must be committed to the grace of God, with a dependence upon and submission to the conduct of that grace (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.12">2 Tim. i. 12</reference>); all our outward concerns must be committed to the providence of God, and to the sovereign, wise, and gracious disposal of that providence. <hi type="italic">Roll thy works upon the Lord</hi> (so the word is); roll the burden of thy care from thyself upon God. Lay the matter before him by prayer. <hi type="italic">Make known thy works unto the Lord</hi> (so some read it), not only the works of thy hand, but the workings of thy heart; and then leave it with him, by faith and dependence upon him, submission and resignation to him. <hi type="italic">The will of the Lord be done.</hi> We may then be easy when we resolve that whatever pleases God shall please us.

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen13964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13965" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath made all <hi type="italic">things</hi> for himself: yea, even the wicked for the day of evil. <div eID="gen13965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13966" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. That God is the first cause. He is the former of all things and all persons, the fountain of being; he gave every creature the being it has and appointed it its place. Even the wicked are his creatures, though they are rebels; he gave them those powers with which they fight against him, which aggravates their wickedness, that they will not let him that made them rule them, and therefore, though he made them, he will not save them. 2. That God is the last end. All is of him and from him, and therefore all is to him and for him. He made all according to his will and for his praise; he designed to serve his own purposes by all his creatures, and he will not fail of his designs; all are his servants. The wicked he is not glorified by, but he will be glorified upon. He makes no man wicked, but he made those who he foresaw would be wicked: yet he made them (<reference osisRef="Gen.6.6">Gen. vi. 6</reference>), because he knew how to <hi type="italic">get himself honour upon them.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Rom.9.22">Rom. ix. 22</reference>. Or (as some understand it) he made the wicked to be employed by him as the instruments of his wrath in the day of evil, when he brings judgments on the world. He makes some use even of wicked men, as of other things, to be his sword, his hand (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.13-Ps.17.14">Ps. xvii. 13, 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">flagellum Dei—the scourge of God.</hi> The king of Babylon is called his <hi type="italic">servant.</hi>

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen13968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13969" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> By mercy and truth iniquity is purged: and by the fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">men</hi> depart from evil. <div eID="gen13969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13970" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen13970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13971" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> When a man's ways please the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him. <div eID="gen13971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13972" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. God can turn foes into friends when he pleases. He that has all hearts in his hand has access to men's spirits and power over them, working insensibly, but irresistibly upon them, can make <hi type="italic">a man's enemies to be at peace with him,</hi> can change their minds, or force them into a feigned submission. He can slay all enemies, and bring those together that were at the greatest distance from each other. 2. He will do it for us when we please him. If we make it our care to be reconciled to God, and to keep ourselves in his love, he will incline those that have been envious towards us, and vexatious to us, to entertain a good opinion of us and to become our friends. God made Esau to be at peace with Jacob, Abimelech with Isaac, and David's enemies to court his favour and desire a league with Israel. The image of God appearing upon the righteous, and his particular lovingkindness to them, are enough to recommend them to the respect of all, even of those that have been most prejudiced against them.

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen13972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13973" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Better <hi type="italic">is</hi> a little with righteousness than great revenues without right. <div eID="gen13973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13974" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. It is supposed that an honest good man may have but a little of the wealth of this world (all the righteous are not rich),—that a man may have but little, and yet may be honest (though poverty is a temptation to dishonesty, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.9">ch. xxx. 9</reference>, yet not an invincible one),—and that a man may grow rich, for a while, by fraud and oppression, may have <hi type="italic">great revenues,</hi> and those got and kept <hi type="italic">without right,</hi> may have no good title to them nor make any good use of them. 2. It is maintained that a small estate, honestly come by, which a man is content with, enjoys comfortably, serves God with cheerfully, and puts to a right use, is much better and more valuable than a great estate ill-got, and then ill-kept or ill-spent. It carries with it more inward satisfaction, a better reputation with all that are wise and good; it will last longer, and will turn to a better account in the great day, when men will be judged, not according to what they had, but what they did.

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen13984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13985" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> The wrath of a king <hi type="italic">is as</hi> messengers of death: but a wise man will pacify it. <hi type="super">15</hi> In the light of the king's countenance <hi type="italic">is</hi> life; and his favour <hi type="italic">is</hi> as a cloud of the latter rain. <div eID="gen13985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13986" type="x-p"/> These two verses show the power of kings, which is every where great, but was especially so in those eastern countries, where they were absolute and arbitrary. Whom they would they slew and whom they would they kept alive. Their will was a law. We have reason to bless God for the happy constitution of the government we live under, which maintains the prerogative of the prince without any injury to the liberty of the subject. But here it is intimated, 1. How formidable <hi type="italic">the wrath of a king is:</hi> It is <hi type="italic">as messengers of death;</hi> the wrath of Ahasuerus was so to Haman. An angry word from an incensed prince has been to many a <hi type="italic">messenger of death,</hi> and has struck so great a terror upon some as if a sentence of death had been pronounced upon them. He must be a very <hi type="italic">wise man</hi> that knows how to <hi type="italic">pacify</hi> the wrath of a king with a word fitly spoken, as Jonathan once pacified his father's rage against David, <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.6">1 Sam. xix. 6</reference>. A prudent subject may sometimes suggest that to an angry prince which will cool his resentments. 2. How valuable and desirable the king's favour is to those that have incurred his displeasure; it is life from the dead if the king be reconciled to them. To others it is <hi type="italic">as a cloud of the latter rain,</hi> very refreshing to the ground. Solomon put his subjects in mind of this, that they might not do any thing to incur his wrath, but be careful to recommend themselves to his favour. We ought by it to be put in mind how much we are concerned to escape the wrath and obtain the favour of the King of kings. His frowns are worse than death, and his favour is better than life; and therefore those are fools who to escape the wrath, and obtain the favour, of an earthly prince, will throw themselves out of God's favour, and make themselves obnoxious to his wrath.  <div eID="gen13986" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv40"/><title type="x-s3">Pride and Humility.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv40"/> <div sID="gen13987" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> How much better <hi type="italic">is it</hi> to get wisdom than gold! and to get understanding rather to be chosen than silver! <div eID="gen13987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13988" type="x-p"/> Solomon here not only asserts that it is better to get wisdom than gold (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.14">ch. iii. 14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.19">viii. 19</reference>), but he speaks it with assurance, that it is much better, better beyond expression—with admiration (<hi type="italic">How much better!</hi>) as one amazed at the disproportion—with an appeal to men's consciences ("Judge in yourselves how much better it is" )—and with an addition to the same purport, that understanding is <hi type="italic">rather to be chosen than silver</hi> and all the treasures of kings and their favourites. Note, 1. Heavenly wisdom is better than worldly wealth, and to be preferred before it. Grace is more valuable than gold. Grace is the gift of God's peculiar favour; gold only of common providence. Grace is for ourselves; gold for others. Grace is for the soul and eternity; gold only for the body and time. Grace will stand us in stead in a dying hour, when gold will do us no good. 2. The getting of this heavenly wisdom is better than the getting of worldly wealth. Many take care and pains to get wealth, and yet come short of it; but grace was never denied to any that sincerely sought it. There is vanity and vexation of spirit in getting wealth, but joy and satisfaction of spirit in getting wisdom. <hi type="italic">Great peace have those that love it.</hi>

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen13988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13989" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> The highway of the upright <hi type="italic">is</hi> to depart from evil: he that keepeth his way preserveth his soul. <div eID="gen13989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13990" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is <hi type="italic">the way of the upright</hi> to avoid sin, and every thing that looks like it and leads towards it; and this is a highway marked out by authority, tracked by many that have gone before us, and in which we meet with many that keep company with us; it is easy to find and safe to be travelled in, like a highway, <reference osisRef="Isa.35.8">Isa. xxxv. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">To depart from evil is understanding.</hi> 2. entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen14000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14001" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> The heart of the wise teacheth his mouth, and addeth learning to his lips. <div eID="gen14001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14002" type="x-p"/> Solomon had commended eloquence, or <hi type="italic">the sweetness of the lips</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.16.21">v. 21</reference>), and seemed to prefer it before wisdom; but here he corrects himself, as it were, and shows that unless there be a good treasure within to support the eloquence it is worth little. Wisdom in <hi type="italic">the heart</hi> is the main matter. 1. It is this that directs us in speaking, that <hi type="italic">teaches the mouth</hi> what to speak, and when, and how, so that what is spoken may be proper, and pertinent, and seasonable; otherwise, though the language be ever so fine, it had better be unsaid. 2. It is this that gives weight to what we speak and <hi type="italic">adds learning</hi> to it, strength of reason and force of argument, without which, let a thing be ever so well worded, it will be rejected, when it comes to be considered, as trifling. Quaint expressions please the ear, and humour the fancy, but it is learning in the lips that must convince the judgment, and sway that, to which wisdom in the heart is necessary.
